title: Lecture #40: Java Stream Methods Deep Dive
topics: Intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, peek)
Terminal operations (reduce, count, match, find, primitive sum/average)
Collectors (toList, toSet, toMap, groupingBy + mapping, partitioningBy, joining)

questions.question: Which of these stream methods is a terminal operation?
questions.explanation: `count()` ends the pipeline and returns a `long`, so it is a terminal (reducing) operation. `peek()` is the tempting wrong answer because it performs an action like `forEach`, but it returns a Stream and is an intermediate operation meant for debugging.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `joining("-")` concatenates the elements in encounter order, the order of the source list, and puts the delimiter only between neighbours. It does not sort or group the strings, so "AA-DD-BBB-EEE-CCCC" (ordered by length) is wrong. The delimiter is not ignored either, which rules out "AABBBCCCCDDEEE".

questions.question: An API shows results 10 per page. To return page 3 (items 21-30) from a stream of results, which pair of operations is correct?
questions.explanation: Skip the first two pages (20 items), then take the next 10. The order matters: `limit(10).skip(20)` first cuts the stream down to 10 items and then skips 20 of them, which leaves an empty result.

questions.question: What value is printed?
questions.explanation: The first argument of `reduce` is the identity (starting value), so the result is 1 + 1 + 13 + 11 + 9 = 35. Answering 34 assumes the identity is ignored. The correct identity for a sum is 0; using 1 is a bug that shifts the result.

questions.question: For `List<List<Integer>> list2 = List.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3, 4));`, the lecture writes `list2.stream().flatMap(x -> x.stream()).map(x -> x * 2)`. Why is `flatMap` needed before `map(x -> x * 2)`?
options: Each element of `list2.stream()` is a `List<Integer>`; `flatMap` replaces each list with its elements, giving one `Stream<Integer>` of 1, 2, 3, 4
`flatMap` sorts the inner lists, and `map` needs sorted input
`flatMap` removes duplicates across the inner lists before `map` runs
`map` cannot be the second operation in a pipeline, so `flatMap` is a required first step
questions.explanation: `flatMap` takes a function that returns a Stream for each element and merges all those streams into one flat stream. With plain `map(x -> x.stream())` you would get a `Stream<Stream<Integer>>`, and `x * 2` would not compile because `x` would be a list, not a number.

questions.question: From `List.of("AA", "BBB", "CCCC", "DD", "EEE")` you need a map from word length to the lowercase words of that length (for example 3 -> [bbb, eee]). Which collector does this?
questions.explanation: `groupingBy` takes a classifier (length) and a downstream collector. `mapping` turns each word into lowercase before collecting it into a list. `toMap` looks close, but it allows only one value per key: "AA" and "DD" share key 2, so it throws `IllegalStateException` (duplicate key). `partitioningBy` needs a boolean predicate.

questions.question: A validator checks `orders.stream().allMatch(o -> o.isPaid())` and `orders.stream().anyMatch(o -> o.isPaid())`. If `orders` is an empty list, what do the two calls return?
options: Both throw `NoSuchElementException`, because there is nothing to test
questions.explanation: On an empty stream, `allMatch` is vacuously true, because no element fails the predicate. `anyMatch` is false, because no element satisfies it. Many developers expect `allMatch` to be false here; if "at least one order, and all paid" is the rule, add an explicit emptiness check.

questions.question: This is the lecture's Demo.java pipeline. What exactly does it print, line by line?
questions.explanation: 11, 34 and 13 pass the filter and become 22, 68, 26. `sorted()` is stateful: it has to receive every element before it can emit any. So `peek` prints 22, 68, 26 first, and then `forEach` prints the sorted values 22, 26, 68. The interleaved "22 22 68 68 26 26" is what you would see without `sorted()`, when each element passes straight through.

questions.question: A report splits order amounts into even and odd with `Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> mp = list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(x -> x % 2 == 0));` and then calls `mp.get(true).size()`. When every amount is odd, this throws a `NullPointerException`. Which change fixes it with the least code?
options: Use `Collectors.partitioningBy(x -> x % 2 == 0)`, because the result always contains both the `true` and `false` keys, so `get(true)` returns an empty list
Use `Collectors.toSet()` instead, because sets never return null for missing elements
Add `.distinct()` before `collect`, so that `groupingBy` creates both keys
Use `Collectors.groupingBy(x -> x % 2)`, because integer keys are always pre-filled
questions.explanation: `groupingBy` only creates keys for classifications that actually occur, so with no even numbers there is no `true` key and `get(true)` returns null. `partitioningBy` always produces a map with both `false` and `true`, with empty lists where nothing matched. Adding `distinct()` changes nothing about which keys appear.

questions.question: The lecture marks `sorted()` and `distinct()` as stateful. Given that, why does `Stream.iterate(1, x -> x + 1).limit(5).sorted().forEach(System.out::println)` print 1-5, while `Stream.iterate(1, x -> x + 1).sorted().limit(5).forEach(System.out::println)` prints nothing and never finishes?
options: `limit` is a terminal operation, so in the second pipeline nothing after it runs
`sorted()` can only sort streams of at most `Integer.MAX_VALUE` elements, so it waits for more input
`sorted()` must see every upstream element before emitting the first; on an infinite stream that never happens, whereas `limit(5)` first makes the input finite
`iterate` produces elements in random order, so `sorted()` keeps re-sorting as new elements arrive
questions.explanation: A stateful operation like `sorted()` buffers its whole input, because the smallest element could arrive last. Before an infinite source, it keeps buffering until memory runs out and never emits anything. Putting `limit(5)` first makes the input finite. `limit` is not terminal: it is a short-circuiting intermediate operation.
